senses.en: a meal; food (吃饭 'to eat, have a meal')
cooked rice (on a menu it is usually 米饭; a bowl of it is 一碗饭)

measure.note: 一顿饭 'a meal'; a bowl of rice is 一碗饭 (碗 wǎn)

examples.en: Food's ready, come and eat!
examples.analysis: 饭 is the whole meal here, not just the rice: 饭好了 'the food is ready' is the call at home when the meal is on the table. 好了 = 'done, ready'. 快来吃吧 urges 'come and eat, quick'.

examples.en: The food here is really good.
examples.analysis: 饭 means the food a place serves. 这儿的饭 = 'the food of this place': the describer 这儿 comes first and 的 links it to 饭. 真 + adjective is an exclamation, 'really tasty'.

examples.en: Let's get a meal together.
examples.analysis: 吃饭 is verb 吃 + object 饭, so a word can go between them. 个 in 吃个饭 makes it sound light and casual, like 'grab a meal'. 吧 makes it a suggestion: a standard way to invite a friend or colleague.

collocations.en: to eat; to have a meal

related.en: plain cooked rice; what you order at a restaurant
dishes eaten with the rice; vegetables

senses.en: this year (a time word, placed before the verb)

examples.en: My son is eight this year.
examples.analysis: 今年 is a time word; here it sits after the subject and before what it times: 我儿子 + 今年 + 八岁 (it could also open the sentence). No 是 is needed with an age: 八岁 works as the predicate by itself.

examples.zh: 今年的生日你想怎么过？
examples.en: How do you want to spend your birthday this year?
examples.analysis: With 的, 今年 describes a noun: 今年的生日 'this year's birthday'. That phrase comes first as the topic, then the question 你想怎么过 'how do you want to spend it'. 过 here means to spend or celebrate a day.

examples.zh: 今年太忙了，明年再去吧。
examples.en: This year is too busy; let's go next year.
examples.analysis: 今年 stands at the front as the topic: 'this year, it's too busy'. It contrasts with 明年 'next year'. 再 here means 'then, and not before': 明年再去 = 'put off going until next year'.

hook: 今 'now, this' (as in 今天 'today') + 年 'year'.

senses.en: left; on its own mainly in short direction talk (左还是右？)
left- before a body part or in a few set words: 左手 'left hand', 左边 'left side'

examples.zh: 从左到右是爸爸、妈妈和我。
examples.en: From left to right: my dad, my mom and me.
examples.analysis: Describing a photo. 从…到… = 'from…to…', and bare 左 and 右 fill the two slots. 是 then lists who is in the picture. 爸爸 and 妈妈 need no 我的 'my' when it is clear whose parents they are; the final 我 is 'me'.

examples.en: At the next intersection, left or right?
examples.analysis: A taxi driver's quick question. Bare 左 works because the action ('turn') is obvious from the situation. 还是 joins two choices into an 'A or B?' question, which takes no 吗.

examples.en: He writes with his left hand.
examples.analysis: 左 goes straight before a body part to mean 'left…': 左手 'left hand' (also 左脚 'left foot'). 用 + tool + action = 'do something with': 用左手写字 'write with the left hand'. Chinese puts the tool before the verb.

collocations.en: about, roughly (after a number: 十点左右)

related.en: the left side; the usual word for a location

senses.en: the place where an event happens or people meet; venue, location

examples.en: Where's the meeting being held?
examples.analysis: 地点 is the place fixed for an event. 开会的地点 = 'the place of the meeting': event + 的 + 地点. 在哪儿 asks where that place is.

examples.zh: 时间和地点我明天告诉你。
examples.en: I'll tell you the time and place tomorrow.
examples.analysis: 时间和地点 'time and place' is the usual pair when planning anything. Here it comes first as the topic, and the comment follows: 我明天告诉你 'I'll tell you tomorrow'. English keeps it after the verb.

examples.en: I don't know the location yet.
examples.analysis: Here 地点 is a plain object, after the verb 知道. 还不知道 = 'still don't know', that is, 'don't know yet'; 呢 at the end goes with 还 and marks a situation that is still open.

hook: 地 'place, ground' + 点 'point': the exact spot.

senses.en: right; on its own mainly in short direction talk (是右，不是左)
right- before a noun: 右手 'right hand', 右边 'right side'

examples.en: No, it's the right, not the left!
examples.analysis: A quick correction, for example to a driver who is about to turn the wrong way. 是右 'it's right' and 不是左 'not left' set the two directions side by side. 不对 'that's wrong' opens the correction.

examples.en: Can you move your right hand?
examples.analysis: 右 goes straight before the noun: 右手 'right hand'. 你右手 is the topic, and 能动吗 asks 'can (it) move?'. A typical question when a doctor checks an injury.

examples.en: A bit more to the right... OK, right there!
examples.analysis: Guiding someone who is placing something, like a picture on a wall. 右 + 一点儿 = 'a bit to the right'; 再 adds 'more'. The full form is 再往右一点儿 with 往 'toward', but quick directions often drop it. 就这儿 is literally 'just here'; English says 'right there' in this situation.

related.en: the right side; the usual word for a location

senses.en: female student; schoolgirl
girl, young woman (in casual everyday speech, not only at school)

examples.en: Our class has more girls than boys.
examples.analysis: 女生 is the subject of a comparison: A 比 B 多 = 'A is more (in number) than B'. 我们班 'our class' sets a school scene, where 女生 and 男生 are the usual words for female and male students.

examples.en: Who's that girl?
examples.analysis: 那个 + noun = 'that…': 那个女生 'that girl'. 是谁 'is who?' asks who she is. Outside school, 女生 is also the casual word for a girl or young woman, much like English 'girl'.

examples.en: I don't know this girl.
examples.analysis: 这个女生 is put first as the topic, and the comment follows: 我不认识 'I'm not acquainted with (her)'. 认识 is knowing a person; moving the object to the front is common in speech when pointing someone out.

hook: 女 'female' + 生 as in 学生 'student'.

senses.en: last time; the previous occasion (a time word)

examples.en: I was in the wrong last time. I'm sorry.
examples.analysis: 上次 opens the sentence and sets the time. 是我不对 = 'it was me who was wrong': 是 points at who was at fault. A natural way to apologize for an earlier argument or mistake.

examples.en: What was that restaurant from last time called?
examples.analysis: 上次 stands right before 那个饭店 and describes it: 'that restaurant (we went to) last time'. In speech a 的 is not needed here. 叫什么 asks for a name: 'is called what?'.

examples.en: The last time we met was last year.
examples.analysis: 上次 goes before the verb it times: 我们上次见面 'our last meeting' is the subject. 是去年 then says when that was, with 是 linking the event to its time.

hook: 上 'previous' (as in 上星期 'last week') + 次 'time, occurrence'.

senses.en: table (for eating, meetings)
desk (for writing or working)

examples.en: Your phone's on the table.
examples.analysis: Thing + 在 + place says where something is. 桌子 alone is just an object; adding 上 'on' turns it into a place, 桌子上 'on the table'. Chinese needs that 上 where English uses the preposition 'on'.

examples.en: Do you have a bigger table?
examples.analysis: Asked in a restaurant. 大一点儿的 'a bit bigger' describes 桌子, linked by 的. 有…吗 'is there…?' is the usual way to ask whether something is available.

examples.en: Don't sit on the table!
examples.analysis: 别 + verb is a 'don't' command. 坐在 + place = 'sit on, sit at'; 桌子上 again makes the table a location. A typical line to a child.

hook: 桌 'table' + the noun ending 子.

senses.en: airport

examples.en: I'm at the airport now. Where are you?
examples.analysis: 到 + place + 了 = 'have arrived at': 我到机场了 'I've arrived at the airport'. 机场 is the place reached. 你在哪儿 'where are you?' is the natural next line when meeting someone there.

examples.en: Is it far from here to the airport?
examples.analysis: 从 A 到 B = 'from A to B', with 机场 as the end point. 远 'far' is the predicate and 吗 makes it a yes/no question. Useful with a taxi driver or at a hotel desk.

examples.zh: 明天我开车送你去机场。
examples.en: I'll drive you to the airport tomorrow.
examples.analysis: 送 + person + 去 + place = 'take someone to a place, see them off'. 开车 in front says how: by car. 机场 is the destination after 去.

collocations.en: pick someone up at the airport

hook: 机, short for 飞机 'plane', + 场 'open ground, field'.

meaning: grandpa (father's father); polite address for an old man

senses.en: grandfather on the father's side; grandpa
a respectful way for children and younger people to address an elderly man (often 老爷爷)

measure.note: 那位老爷爷 'that old gentleman' (位 is the polite measure)

examples.en: Grandpa, have a seat here.
examples.analysis: 爷爷 is used to call him, at the start like a name. 您 is the respectful 'you', and 吧 softens the request. Young people also say this when offering a seat to an elderly man on a bus, since 爷爷 is a polite address for men of grandparent age.

examples.en: Grandpa isn't home; he's gone out.
examples.analysis: 爷爷 is the subject of both parts; the second part drops it because it is clear. 不在家 = 'not at home'. 出去了 = 'has gone out', with 了 marking that it has happened.

examples.zh: 我爷爷八十岁了，身体还很好。
examples.en: My grandpa is eighty and still in good health.
examples.analysis: 我爷爷 = 'my grandpa', with no 的, as with other close family. 八十岁了 = 'is eighty now': 了 marks the age reached. 身体还很好 'is still in good health'; 还 = 'still'.

related.en: grandpa on the mother's side (northern; also 外公 wàigōng)

senses.en: dinner, supper; the evening meal

examples.en: What's for dinner?
examples.analysis: 晚饭 comes first as the topic, 'as for dinner', then 吃什么 'eat what?'. No subject is needed because everyone knows who is eating. The everyday question at home when planning the evening meal.

examples.en: I'm not having dinner at home today.
examples.analysis: 晚饭 is placed before the subject as the topic. 不 + 在家 + 吃 = 'not eat at home': the place phrase comes before the verb, and 不 goes before the whole phrase. A typical message to family.

examples.en: Let's have dinner at seven.
examples.analysis: 吃晚饭 'have dinner': 晚饭 is the object of 吃. The clock time 七点 goes before the verb, not at the end as in English 'at seven'. 吧 turns it into a suggestion.

senses.en: the middle, the center (坐中间 'sit in the middle')
between: A 和 B 中间 'between A and B'
partway through a period (中间休息 'a break in the middle')

examples.en: I'll sit in the middle.
examples.analysis: 中间 is a place word, so it can follow 坐 directly: 坐中间 'sit in the middle' (a fuller form is 坐在中间). 吧 makes it an offer: 'I'll take the middle, OK?'

examples.zh: 商店就在医院和学校中间。
examples.en: The shop is right between the hospital and the school.
examples.analysis: A 和 B 中间 = 'between A and B': the two places come first, then 中间. 在 + this place phrase says where the shop is; 就 adds 'right, just'.

examples.en: Who's the person in the middle?
examples.analysis: 中间 describes 那个人 directly, with no 的: 'the person in the middle', for example in a photo. 是谁 'is who?' asks who that is.

senses.en: to sing; to sing songs (verb 唱 + object 歌)
去唱歌: to go out singing, often at a karaoke (KTV) place

examples.en: Let's go sing tonight!
examples.analysis: 去 + 唱歌 = 'go and sing': the purpose comes straight after 去. Among friends in China, 去唱歌 often means going to a karaoke (KTV) place. 吧 makes it a suggestion.

examples.en: She sings beautifully.
examples.analysis: 她唱歌 'her singing' is the topic, and 很好听 'is lovely to hear' is the comment. English uses an adverb ('beautifully'); Chinese describes the singing with an adjective instead.

examples.en: I can't sing. You sing.
examples.analysis: 会 = 'know how to', so 不会唱歌 = 'can't sing'. In the second half 唱 stands alone: 唱歌 is verb 唱 + object 歌, and when the object is clear, 唱 is enough.

hook: 唱 'to sing' + 歌 'song': a verb with its object.

senses.en: electricity; power supply (停电 'power cut')
battery charge (手机没电了 'my phone is dead')

examples.en: My phone's dead.
examples.analysis: 电 is the power, here the battery charge. 没电了 = 'has no power now': 没 'not have' + 电, with 了 marking the change. 我手机 drops 的, which is common in casual speech.

examples.en: How much battery does your computer have left?
examples.analysis: 电 is the object: 有多少电 'have how much power'. 还 'still' makes it 'how much is left'. 多少 asks for an amount, so no 吗 is needed.

examples.en: Don't touch it, it's live!
examples.analysis: 有电 = 'there is current in it', a warning about a live wire or socket. 别动 'don't touch, don't move it' comes first; the command is given, then the reason.

senses.en: train (railway)

examples.en: What time does the train leave?
examples.analysis: 火车 is the subject. With a train or bus as the subject, 开 means 'to leave, set off' (with a person as the subject, 开车 is 'to drive'). The time question 几点 goes before the verb, exactly where the answer will go: 火车八点开 'the train leaves at eight'.

examples.en: Let's take the train to Beijing.
examples.analysis: 坐 + vehicle = 'travel by': 坐火车 'by train'. The means comes first, then 去 + place: 坐火车去北京 'go to Beijing by train'. 吧 marks a suggestion.

examples.en: There are way too many people on the train.
examples.analysis: 火车上 = 'on the train': 上 turns the vehicle into a place. The place comes first, then what is there: 人太多了 'too many people'. Here 太…了 is a complaint that there are too many; with a positive word (太好了) it is praise instead.

related.en: high-speed train, high-speed rail (often contrasted with ordinary 火车)

hook: 火 'fire' + 车 'vehicle': the name comes from early steam trains, which ran on burning fuel.

meaning: wrong, incorrect; (as a reply) no, that's not right

senses.en: wrong, incorrect (钱不对 'the money's wrong')
(as a reply) no, that's not right
not normal; something's off (不太对 'not quite right')

examples.en: The money isn't right. It's ten yuan short.
examples.analysis: 不对 is the predicate: 钱不对 'the money is wrong'. The second part says how: 少了十块 'ten short'. 块 is the spoken word for yuan.

examples.en: No, not this one. That one.
examples.analysis: 不对 stands alone at the start as a reply: 'No, that's wrong'. Then 不是…是… corrects it: 'not this, but that'. Handy when someone picks up the wrong item for you.

examples.en: Is what I said wrong?
examples.analysis: 我说的 'what I said' is the subject: verb + 的 makes 'the thing said'. 不对 + 吗 asks 'is it wrong?'. Depending on tone, it is a real question or a mild challenge.

collocations.en: right? is it right or not?
not quite right; a bit off

meaning: on the floor; on the ground

senses.en: on the floor; on the ground (a place word)

examples.en: There's water all over the floor.
examples.analysis: 地上 'on the floor' is the place, put first. 都是 + thing = 'is all…, covered in…'. Place + 是 or 有 + thing is how Chinese says what is somewhere.

examples.en: Don't sit on the floor, it's too cold.
examples.analysis: 坐 + 地上 = 'sit on the floor'; a fuller form is 坐在地上, but speech often drops 在. 地上 already contains 上 'on', so no other word is needed. 别 makes it a 'don't'.

examples.en: Whose bag is that on the floor?
examples.analysis: 地上 describes 那个包: 'that bag on the floor'. 是谁的 'is whose?' asks for the owner; 谁的 works like 'whose' standing alone.

collocations.en: to fall on the floor (of something dropped)

senses.en: lunch; the midday meal

examples.en: Have you had lunch?
examples.analysis: 午饭 comes first as the topic: '(as for) lunch, eaten?'. 'You' is dropped because it is obvious who is being asked, not because of the word order. 吃了吗 asks whether it has happened. Around noon this also works as a friendly greeting.

examples.en: Lunch is on me today!
examples.analysis: 请 here means 'to treat, pay for someone'. 午饭 is the topic, placed before 我请 'I'll treat'. A standard way to offer to pay.

examples.en: Too busy. No time for lunch.
examples.analysis: 吃午饭 'eat lunch': 午饭 is the object. 没时间 + verb = 'no time to do it'; the action simply follows 时间. There is no subject: context makes it 'I'.

hook: 午 'noon' (as in 中午) + 饭 'meal'.

meaning: some (of a group); some people or things

senses.en: some (of a group): 有的人 'some people'
有的…，有的… 'some…, others…'

examples.en: Some of the classmates haven't arrived yet.
examples.analysis: 有的 + noun = 'some (of the)…': 有的同学 'some classmates'. It sits before the noun at the front of the sentence. 还没来 = 'haven't come yet'.

examples.zh: 这些菜有的好吃，有的不好吃。
examples.en: Some of these dishes are tasty, and some aren't.
examples.analysis: 有的…，有的… = 'some…, others…'. 这些菜 'these dishes' is the topic, and each 有的 picks out part of it. Here 有的 stands alone, with the noun understood.

examples.en: Some people don't eat meat. What about you?
examples.analysis: 有的人 'some people' is the subject. 有的 normally comes before the verb; for 'some' after a verb, Chinese uses 一些 (我买了一些). 你呢 'and you?' turns it into a polite question about the listener's diet.

related.en: some, a few (also after the verb)

senses.en: east; east- before a noun (东门 'east gate', 东边 'the east side')

examples.en: I'll wait for you at the east gate.
examples.analysis: 东 + noun = 'east…': 东门 'east gate'. Parks, campuses, hospitals and housing compounds in China often name their gates 东门, 西门, 南门, 北门, so this is how people fix a meeting point. 在 + place + 等 = 'wait at'.

examples.en: Are you going to the East Station or the West Station?
examples.analysis: 东站 'East Station'. Many Chinese cities have several railway stations named by direction, so a taxi driver may ask this. 还是 asks 'A or B?', with no 吗.

examples.zh: 学校太大了，从东到西要走半天。
examples.en: The campus is so big; walking from east to west takes ages.
examples.analysis: 从东到西 'from east to west': bare 东 and 西 fill the 从…到… frame, as 左 and 右 do. 要 here means 'it takes': 要走半天 'it takes a long while to walk'. 半天 in casual speech often means 'a long while', as it does here, not literally half a day.

collocations.en: the east side; to the east
